newsitem.title: USA: Analysts see slight cut in USDA soy ending stocks.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see slight cut in USDA soy ending stocks.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department will trim only slightly its 1996-97 ending soybean stocks projection in Friday's supply and demand report, oilseeds analysts said.
"I think they'll (stocks) be down a little bit," said Dale Gustafson, analyst with Smith Barney. "Maybe five to 10 million bushels. They'll increase residual use and increase imports."
USDA in March put soybean stocks at 140 million bushels. The April report is due Friday at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT.

Analysts said lofty U.S. soybean prices were attracting cheap, abundant South American soybeans north and could push USDA to raise U.S. soybean imports to 10 million bushels from roughly four million in the March report.
One vessel carrying roughly 1.9 million bushels of soybeans was sent from Brazil on March 31. A shipping agent said it was headed for New Orleans.

"They'll probably raise the bean imports," said Dan Cekander, head of grain research for FIMAT Futures in Chicago. "They could raise the crush slightly and lower the exports slightly in beans but only minor adjustments."

USDA put export usage at 900 million bushels as of March 1 but soybean prices at the Chicago Board of Trade have rallied more than 50 cents per bushel since then and some potential buyers may have backed away or shifted purchases into the next crop year, Cekander said.
The soybean marketing year runs from September 1 to August 31. Soybeans for May delivery closed at $8.62-3/4 per bushel on Monday but new crop November soybeans were at $7.05.
"My feeling is that the large inverse between old and new crop will lead to some shifting of demand from the old to new crop," Cekander said.
Demand from Taiwan was also expected to falter after an outbreak of foot and mouth disease forced them to decimate the hog population, said Dave Armstrong, analyst with ABN-AMRO Chicago Corp.
"Taiwan is going to delay imports and you could end up taking 10 (million bushels) out of there," he said.
Analysts rejected theories USDA would shave 22 million bushels off the ending soybean stocks after last week's downward revision to the March 1 quarterly stocks figure.
USDA on April 1 corrected its quarterly stocks figure (as of March 1) to 1.056 billion bushels, down 22 million bushels from the initial number of 1.078 billion.
